opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the progress has been striking, and it's worth being precise about what kind of progress it is.

A few years ago, the headline was multiple-choice medical exams. Models went from barely passing USMLE-style questions to matching and then exceeding expert-level scores fairly quickly. That was an important signal, but those benchmarks were never the real goal. Real health conversations are messy. People describe symptoms vaguely, leave out key context, are anxious, or are asking on behalf of a parent or a child. The question is whether a model can handle *that* well.

So much of the field's attention, including my own, has shifted toward evaluating realistic, open-ended conversations. Does the model ask the right follow-up questions? Does it recognize when something is an emergency and say so clearly? Does it hedge appropriately when there's real uncertainty, without hedging so much that it's useless? Does it tailor its answer to a layperson versus a clinician? On those dimensions, the newer models have improved a lot, in some areas to the point where physicians reviewing responses often prefer the model's answer to one written by a doctor under typical time constraints.

That said, I'd be careful about declaring victory. There are still meaningful gaps. Models can be overconfident, they can miss context that a clinician would pick up on, and performance can be uneven across languages, regions, and populations. And a good answer in an evaluation doesn't automatically translate into better health outcomes. That's the bar we ultimately care about, and it requires real-world studies, not just benchmarks.

So my honest assessment: we've moved from "can models know medicine?" to "can models reliably help people in real situations?" The answer to the first is clearly yes. The answer to the second is "increasingly, and in many cases already meaningfully," but measuring and closing the remaining gaps is where the hard, important work is now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the progress has been genuinely remarkable, and I say that as someone who's been fairly close to the measurement side of it. If you go back just a few years, the state of the art on medical question answering was pretty humbling. Models would score in the fifties on something like USMLE-style questions, and the failure modes were the kind that would make any clinician nervous. They'd hallucinate drug interactions, they'd confidently cite guidelines that didn't exist, and they'd give you an answer that sounded authoritative but had no real grounding.

What's changed is that the models now clear the bar that used to be the whole goal. Passing medical licensing exams, matching or exceeding physician performance on structured benchmarks, that's largely a solved problem for the frontier models. And to be clear, that was a real milestone. It told us the knowledge was in there, that the models had absorbed an enormous amount of the medical literature and could reason over it reasonably well.

But I'd argue the more interesting progress, and the harder progress, has been on the dimensions that don't show up in a multiple-choice score. Does the model know what it doesn't know? Does it ask a clarifying question when the symptoms are ambiguous instead of guessing? Does it recognize when someone needs to go to an emergency room right now versus when it's appropriate to give information and let them decide? Does it communicate in a way that's actually useful to a frightened person at two in the morning, rather than to a resident on rounds?

Those are the things that matter when real people use these systems, and real people are using them. Millions of health conversations happen with AI models every day. So the evaluation has to shift from "can it answer the exam question" to "does it behave well in the messy, high-stakes, emotionally loaded context of someone's actual health." And on that front I'd say we've made serious progress, but we're much earlier in the journey than the benchmark numbers would suggest.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we've learned a lot about how to evaluate. Early on, we relied heavily on automated metrics and benchmarks. Over time, we built out rubrics with physicians, we ran human evaluations where clinicians compared model responses to one another and to what they'd write themselves, and we started paying attention to things like safety, accuracy of the reasoning, and whether the response was appropriately calibrated. That infrastructure is part of why the models got better, because you can't improve what you can't measure. So the story of progress in health AI is partly a story about the models getting stronger, and partly a story about us getting better at asking the right questions of them.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress has been really substantial, but we have to be careful about what we mean by progress. Answering a medical knowledge question correctly is one thing. Helping someone make sense of a health concern, with incomplete information and real consequences, is a much harder problem.

For me, the interesting question is increasingly: Does the model know when to ask a follow-up question? Can it recognize that it doesn’t have enough information? Can it communicate uncertainty in a way that actually helps the person decide what to do next?

So I’m optimistic about the potential, especially for making health information more understandable and accessible. But I wouldn’t equate better performance on a benchmark with being ready to handle every real-world health situation. We need to evaluate the whole interaction, including whether the model recognizes when someone needs professional care.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress has been substantial, but it’s important to separate answering a health question from reliably helping someone make a health decision. Models have gotten much better at understanding medical information, explaining it clearly, and reasoning through complicated questions. Those are useful capabilities.

But a real person’s situation often has missing context. They might not know which symptoms matter, or they might phrase a question in a way that hides the most important issue. A good model needs to recognize that, ask the right follow-up questions, and communicate uncertainty. Sometimes the most helpful answer is, “This could be urgent—you should get medical attention.”

So I’m excited about the trajectory. But I’d assess progress by whether models help people reach better decisions in realistic situations, not just whether they can produce a convincing answer to a medical question.
